nodes.label: Normed Vector Spaces and Equivalent Norms
nodes.explanation: Assumes graduate entry background in real and complex vector spaces, subspaces, linear maps, metric spaces (open and closed sets, closures, convergence, continuity), and standard real/complex inequalities. Develops the norm axioms over K = R or C, the reverse triangle inequality |‖x‖ - ‖y‖| ≤ ‖x - y‖, the induced translation-invariant homogeneous metric d(x, y) = ‖x - y‖, and continuity of vector addition, scalar multiplication, and the norm, together with the fact that the closure of a subspace is a subspace. Introduces core concrete normed spaces—K^n with ‖·‖_1, ‖·‖_2, and ‖·‖_∞; C([a, b]) with ‖·‖_∞ and ‖·‖_1; bounded sequences ℓ^∞ with ‖·‖_∞; and finitely supported sequences c_00—and develops comparison and equivalence of norms (c‖x‖_1 ≤ ‖x‖_2 ≤ C‖x‖_1). Uses scaling and translation of balls as the key bridge to prove two norms are equivalent if and only if they induce the same open sets (equivalently, the same convergent sequences), contrasting the equivalent p-norms on K^n with the inequivalent norms ‖·‖_∞ and ‖·‖_1 on C([0, 1]) via sequences of narrow spike or power functions. Enables the learner to verify norm axioms, establish topological properties of subspaces, and prove or refute equivalence of norms on concrete vector spaces. Leaves completeness, general ℓ^p spaces for 1 < p < ∞, and the theorem that all norms on arbitrary finite-dimensional spaces are equivalent to subsequent lessons.

nodes.label: The Baire Category Theorem in Complete Metric Spaces
nodes.explanation: Assumes graduate entry background in metric spaces (open and closed sets, closures, interiors, dense subsets, Cauchy sequences, and completeness). Introduces nowhere dense sets (sets whose closure has empty interior), meager (first category) sets, and residual sets, and develops both equivalent forms of the Baire Category Theorem: in a complete metric space, every countable intersection of open dense sets is dense, and a nonempty complete metric space cannot be expressed as a countable union of nowhere dense closed sets (equivalently, if X = ⋃ F_n with each F_n closed, then some F_n has nonempty interior). Carries out the nested shrinking closed balls construction (choosing closed balls B[x_{n+1}, r_{n+1}] ⊂ B(x_n, r_n) ∩ U_{n+1} with r_n < 2^{-n}) as the central bridge where completeness produces a common limit point, and contrasts this with incomplete metric spaces such as Q to show completeness is essential. Enables the learner to test nowhere-denseness, prove the Baire Category Theorem, and apply its closed-covering form to metric-space existence and non-decomposition problems (such as showing a complete metric space with no isolated points is uncountable). Stays strictly within complete metric spaces and leaves normed spaces and linear-operator applications (Uniform Boundedness and Open Mapping) to later lessons.

nodes.label: Banach Spaces and the Absolute Convergence Criterion
nodes.explanation: Builds on normed spaces and norm equivalence to define Banach spaces (normed spaces complete in their induced metric) and establish how completeness interacts with linear structure: closed subspaces of Banach spaces are Banach, complete subspaces of normed spaces are closed, and completeness is preserved under equivalent norms. Develops and proves both directions of the absolute convergence criterion—a normed space X is Banach if and only if every absolutely convergent series (∑ ‖x_n‖ < ∞) converges in X—highlighting the subsequence extraction bridge (‖x_{n_{k+1}} - x_{n_k}‖ < 2^{-k}) and telescoping sum used in the converse. Applies direct Cauchy arguments and the series criterion to prove completeness of K^n, ℓ^∞, the closed subspaces c and c_0 (noting c_00 is dense in c_0 but not in ℓ^∞), and C(K) for any compact metric space K under the supremum norm (linking uniform convergence to ‖·‖_∞), while constructing explicit non-convergent Cauchy sequences to refute completeness of (c_00, ‖·‖_∞) and (C([0, 1]), ‖·‖_1). Enables the learner to prove completeness via either Cauchy sequences or absolute series convergence and to construct counterexamples to completeness. Leaves general ℓ^p spaces (1 ≤ p < ∞) and quotient/completion constructions to separate lessons.

nodes.label: Bounded Linear Operators and the Operator Norm
nodes.explanation: Builds on normed spaces and norm equivalence to develop bounded linear operators T : X → Y between normed spaces. Proves the equivalence of continuity, continuity at 0, Lipschitz continuity, and boundedness (‖Tx‖_Y ≤ M‖x‖_X), and derives the equivalent variational formulas for the operator norm ‖T‖ = inf{M : ‖Tx‖ ≤ M‖x‖} = sup_{‖x‖≤1} ‖Tx‖ = sup_{‖x‖=1} ‖Tx‖ (handling X = {0} explicitly). Establishes bounded linear isomorphisms, boundedness below (‖Tx‖ ≥ c‖x‖), and linear isometries, connecting norm equivalence to bounded invertibility of the identity map. Trains the two-step workflow for exact operator-norm computation—proving an upper bound and matching it with a unit vector or a sequence of unit vectors, emphasizing that the supremum need not be attained in infinite dimensions—on matrices on (K^n, ‖·‖_1) and (K^n, ‖·‖_∞), diagonal and shift operators on ℓ^∞, multiplication and integral operators on (C([0, 1]), ‖·‖_∞), and the contrasting unbounded differentiation operator D : (C^1([0, 1]), ‖·‖_∞) → (C([0, 1]), ‖·‖_∞). Enables the learner to distinguish bounded from unbounded linear maps and compute exact operator norms in attained and unattained cases. Leaves the Banach-space structure of B(X, Y), composition, extension from dense subspaces, and the fact that every linear map on an abstract finite-dimensional normed space is bounded to later lessons.

nodes.label: The Sequence Spaces ℓ^p and Hölder-Minkowski Inequalities
nodes.explanation: Builds on Banach spaces and the established spaces c_0 and ℓ^∞, assuming elementary calculus (concavity of ln or convexity of exp), to construct and analyze the classical sequence spaces ℓ^p for 1 ≤ p < ∞. Introduces conjugate exponents (1/p + 1/q = 1 for 1 < p < ∞), proves Young's inequality ab ≤ a^p/p + b^q/q, derives Hölder's inequality for finite sums and infinite series, and establishes Minkowski's inequality to verify that ‖·‖_p is a norm on ℓ^p. Proves completeness of ℓ^p via coordinatewise convergence of Cauchy sequences paired with the finite partial-sum pass-to-the-limit step (showing ∑_{k=1}^N |x_k^{(n)} - x_k|^p ≤ ε^p before letting N → ∞). Establishes the strict nesting inclusions ℓ^p ⊊ ℓ^r ⊊ c_0 ⊊ ℓ^∞ for 1 ≤ p < r < ∞ with ‖x‖_r ≤ ‖x‖_p, proves separability of ℓ^p (1 ≤ p < ∞) and c_0 via rational-coordinate sequences in c_00, and proves non-separability of ℓ^∞ using {0, 1}^N with pairwise distance 1. Enables the learner to manipulate ℓ^p norms via Hölder and Minkowski, verify convergence and completeness in ℓ^p, and compare separability across sequence spaces. Stays strictly in sequence spaces without requiring measure theory or Lebesgue L^p spaces.

nodes.label: Finite-Dimensional Normed Spaces and Riesz's Lemma
nodes.explanation: Builds on Banach spaces and assumes standard finite-dimensional linear algebra and Heine-Borel compactness in K^n to characterize finite-dimensional normed spaces and contrast them with infinite-dimensional geometry. Proves that all norms on a finite-dimensional normed space X are equivalent by fixing a basis {e_1, ..., e_n} and bounding any norm against the coordinate ℓ^1-norm, using continuity on the compact unit sphere S_1 ⊂ K^n as the essential bridge for the lower bound. Deduces that every finite-dimensional normed space is a Banach space, every finite-dimensional subspace of any normed space is closed, and closed bounded sets in finite dimensions are compact. Proves Riesz's Lemma: for any proper closed subspace M of a normed space X and any 0 < θ < 1, there exists a unit vector x_θ with dist(x_θ, M) ≥ θ (explicitly noting that θ = 1 need not be achievable in general normed spaces), and applies it inductively to construct a 1/2-separated sequence in the closed unit ball, proving that the closed unit ball of X is compact if and only if dim X < ∞. Enables the learner to justify closedness and completeness of finite-dimensional subspaces, construct almost-separated unit vectors via Riesz's Lemma, and diagnose failures of finite-dimensional compactness arguments in infinite dimensions.

nodes.label: Direct Sums, Quotient Normed Spaces, and Completeness
nodes.explanation: Builds on Banach spaces and the absolute convergence criterion, assuming basic algebraic quotient vector spaces X/M from linear algebra, to construct new Banach spaces from existing ones. Equips finite products (direct sums) X_1 ⊕ ... ⊕ X_k with equivalent product norms (such as ‖x‖_1, ‖x‖_2, ‖x‖_∞) and verifies completeness when each factor is Banach. Defines the quotient functional ‖x + M‖_{X/M} = inf_{m ∈ M} ‖x - m‖ = dist(x, M) on X/M, proving that it is a seminorm in general and a norm if and only if M is closed in X, and showing that the canonical quotient map π : X → X/M satisfies ‖π(x)‖ ≤ ‖x‖ and maps the open unit ball of X onto the open unit ball of X/M. Proves that if X is Banach and M is a closed subspace, then X/M is a Banach space by applying the absolute convergence criterion (choosing coset representatives y_n ∈ x_n + M with ‖y_n‖ < ‖x_n + M‖ + 2^{-n} so ∑ y_n converges in X), and establishes the converse three-space property (M and X/M Banach imply X Banach). Computes concrete quotient norms such as on c/c_0 and ℓ^∞/c_0 (identifying the quotient norm with limsup |x_n|). Enables the learner to construct and verify completeness of product and quotient Banach spaces and compute quotient norms, leaving completions and bounded-operator factorizations to later lessons.

nodes.label: The Space B(X, Y), Composition, and Extension by Continuity
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes Banach spaces and bounded linear operators to develop the normed-space and Banach-space structure of B(X, Y). Verifies that the operator norm makes B(X, Y) a normed vector space, proves that B(X, Y) is a Banach space whenever the codomain Y is Banach (even when the domain X is incomplete) by passing from Cauchy sequences in operator norm to pointwise limits and passing to the limit inside ‖(T_n - T_m)x‖ ≤ ε‖x‖, and avoids claiming necessity of Y's completeness for arbitrary X before Hahn-Banach is established. Proves that composition of bounded operators is bounded and submultiplicative (‖ST‖ ≤ ‖S‖‖T‖, with examples of strict inequality) and continuous, making B(X) a Banach algebra when X is Banach. Proves the Bounded Linear Transformation (BLT) Extension Theorem: any bounded linear operator T_0 : X_0 → Y from a dense subspace X_0 ⊂ X into a Banach space Y extends uniquely to T ∈ B(X, Y) with ‖T‖ = ‖T_0‖ (preserving isometries), highlighting why completeness of Y is essential. Enables the learner to construct operators as operator-norm limits, bound operator products and powers, and uniquely extend bounded operators defined on dense subspaces such as c_00 ⊂ c_0 or polynomials in C([0, 1]) (citing Weierstrass approximation if used as supplied real-analysis background). Leaves completions, invertibility via Neumann series, and dual spaces to subsequent lessons.

nodes.label: Completion of Normed Spaces
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes quotient normed spaces and the BLT extension theorem to prove that every normed space X admits an essentially unique Banach completion. Constructs the completion X_hat explicitly as the quotient of the space of Cauchy sequences in X by the subspace of null sequences, equipped with ‖(x_n) + N‖ = lim_{n→∞} ‖x_n‖, verifying that vector operations are well-defined, the constant-sequence embedding ι : X → X_hat is a linear isometry with dense image, and X_hat is complete via a diagonal Cauchy-sequence argument. Uses the BLT extension theorem from B(X, Y) to establish the universal property of completion—every bounded linear operator from X into a Banach space Y factors uniquely through X_hat with the same norm—and deduces uniqueness of the completion up to a unique isometric isomorphism fixing X. Applies this uniqueness criterion to identify concrete completions without rebuilding Cauchy sequences from scratch (such as c_00 under ‖·‖_∞ completing to c_0, and piecewise linear functions under ‖·‖_∞ completing to C([0, 1]) using uniform continuity). Enables the learner to identify completions of incomplete normed spaces by exhibiting dense isometric embeddings into Banach spaces and to lift operators from incomplete spaces to their completions. Leaves the alternative bidual realization until canonical embeddings are developed.

nodes.label: Invertible Operators and the Neumann Series
nodes.explanation: Builds on the completeness and submultiplicativity of the Banach algebra B(X) (for a Banach space X) to analyze boundedly invertible operators GL(X) = {T ∈ B(X) : ∃ T^{-1} ∈ B(X)}, noting explicitly that invertibility here includes boundedness of T^{-1} (leaving automatic boundedness of inverses of bijections to the Bounded Inverse Theorem). Proves the Neumann Series Theorem: if X is Banach and T ∈ B(X) satisfies ‖T‖ < 1, then ∑_{n=0}^∞ T^n converges absolutely in B(X) to (I - T)^{-1}, yielding the norm bound ‖(I - T)^{-1}‖ ≤ (1 - ‖T‖)^{-1} and truncation error bound ‖(I - T)^{-1} - ∑_{n=0}^N T^n‖ ≤ ‖T‖^{N+1}/(1 - ‖T‖). Applies Neumann series to S - (S - T) = S(I - S^{-1}(S - T)) to prove perturbation stability: if S ∈ GL(X) and ‖T - S‖ < ‖S^{-1}‖^{-1}, then T ∈ GL(X); deduces that GL(X) is open in B(X) and that inversion S ↦ S^{-1} is continuous on GL(X). Demonstrates concrete use on Fredholm integral equations (I - λK)f = g on C([a, b]) for |λ|‖K‖ < 1 and sensitivity estimates for perturbed linear equations. Enables the learner to prove invertibility under small perturbations, approximate inverses with explicit error bounds, and verify where completeness of X is required. Excludes general spectral theory, resolvent calculus, and compact operators.

nodes.label: Bounded Linear Functionals, Dual Spaces, and Hyperplanes
nodes.explanation: Builds on B(X, Y) (together with established concrete spaces K^n, c_0, c_00, C([0, 1]), and C^1([0, 1]) from earlier ancestors) to introduce the topological dual space X* = B(X, K) with dual norm ‖f‖ = sup_{‖x‖≤1} |f(x)|, noting immediately that X* is a Banach space for every normed space X because K is complete. Contrasts X* with the algebraic dual by exhibiting explicit discontinuous linear functionals on infinite-dimensional normed spaces (such as f(x) = ∑ n x_n on (c_00, ‖·‖_∞) and u ↦ u'(0) on (C^1([0, 1]), ‖·‖_∞)), whereas every linear functional on K^n is bounded. Proves the geometric kernel characterization: a nonzero linear functional f : X → K is continuous if and only if ker f is closed in X, and otherwise ker f is dense in X (using the bridge x_0 - x/f(x) ∈ ker f for a fixed x_0 with f(x_0) = 1 outside a ball avoiding ker f), and establishes that two functionals with the same kernel are scalar multiples. Practices computing exact dual norms of concrete functionals on c_0 and C([0, 1]), including point evaluations, weighted integrals, and an unattained dual norm such as f(u) = ∫_0^{1/2} u - ∫_{1/2}^1 u on C([0, 1]). Enables the learner to test continuity via kernels and compute norms of concrete functionals, leaving full identifications of (c_0)* and (ℓ^p)* and existence theorems for general normed spaces to the next lessons.

nodes.label: Duals of Classical Sequence Spaces: c₀ and ℓ^p
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes the ℓ^p sequence spaces (Hölder's inequality, density of c_00, and non-separability of ℓ^∞) and dual spaces to prove the classical isometric isomorphisms (c_0)* ≅ ℓ^1, (ℓ^1)* ≅ ℓ^∞, and (ℓ^p)* ≅ ℓ^q for 1 < p < ∞ (1/p + 1/q = 1). Carries out the full three-part verification for the pairing map (Φy)(x) = ∑ x_n y_n: upper bound ‖Φy‖ ≤ ‖y‖_q via Hölder's inequality; surjectivity by setting y_n = f(e_n), constructing the critical sign-and-power test vectors x^{(N)} = ∑_{n=1}^N sgn(conj(y_n)) |y_n|^{q-1} e_n (or sgn(conj(y_n)) e_n for c_0) to establish ‖y‖_q ≤ ‖f‖, and invoking density of c_00 in c_0 and ℓ^p to conclude f = Φy; and equality of norms ‖Φy‖ = ‖y‖_q. Diagnoses precisely why the proof breaks for ℓ^∞: c_00 is not dense in ℓ^∞, so Φ : ℓ^1 → (ℓ^∞)* is an isometry, while the limit functional L(x) = lim x_n on c ⊂ ℓ^∞ vanishes on c_00 yet satisfies L(1, 1, ...) = 1, foreshadowing functionals in (ℓ^∞)* outside ℓ^1. Enables the learner to represent bounded functionals on c_0 and ℓ^p explicitly, compute their exact norms via conjugate norms, and explain why (ℓ^∞)* is not captured by ℓ^1. Leaves existence of extensions of L to all of ℓ^∞ to Hahn-Banach and avoids measure-theoretic L^p duals.

nodes.label: The Analytic Hahn-Banach Extension Theorem
nodes.explanation: Builds on bounded linear functionals and dual spaces, explicitly assuming Zorn's Lemma on partially ordered sets (chains, upper bounds, maximal elements) as graduate set-theoretic background, to prove the analytic Hahn-Banach extension theorems. Introduces sublinear functionals and seminorms, and proves the real Hahn-Banach theorem: a linear functional f_0 on a subspace M dominated by a sublinear functional p extends to a p-dominated linear functional on all of X. Develops both essential bridges: the one-dimensional extension step to M ⊕ R x_0 verifying sup_{y∈M}(f_0(y) - p(y - x_0)) ≤ inf_{z∈M}(p(z + x_0) - f_0(z)) so an admissible value f(x_0) exists, and the Zorn's Lemma maximality argument on the poset of dominated extensions. Derives the complex Hahn-Banach theorem for a seminorm p by applying the real theorem to u_0 = Re f_0, reconstructing f(x) = u(x) - i u(ix), and using phase rotation e^{-iθ} f(x) = |f(x)| = u(e^{-iθ} x) ≤ p(x) to verify domination. Deduces the norm-preserving extension corollary for any real or complex normed space: every f_0 ∈ M* extends to f ∈ X* with ‖f‖_{X*} = ‖f_0‖_{M*}. Applies the theorem to extend the limit functional from c to ℓ^∞ (using c and ℓ^∞ established earlier) and exhibits non-uniqueness of norm-preserving extensions (for instance on (R^2, ‖·‖_∞)). Enables the learner to carry out dominated one-step extensions, prove real and complex Hahn-Banach, and construct norm-preserving extensions, leaving separation theorems and annihilators to the next lesson.

nodes.label: Norming Functionals, Subspace Separation, and Annihilators
nodes.explanation: Builds on the analytic Hahn-Banach extension theorem (and uses ℓ^∞ established in earlier ancestors) to derive the core structural consequences of Hahn-Banach for normed spaces and their duals. Proves the existence of norming functionals (for every nonzero x_0 ∈ X, some f ∈ X* satisfies ‖f‖ = 1 and f(x_0) = ‖x_0‖), the attained dual norm formula ‖x‖ = max_{‖f‖≤1} |f(x)|, and point separation by X*. Proves separation of a point x_0 from a closed subspace M with d = dist(x_0, M) > 0 by defining f_0(m + λx_0) = λd on M ⊕ K x_0, verifying |f_0(m + λx_0)| = |λ|d ≤ ‖m + λx_0‖, and extending to f ∈ X* with f|_M = 0, f(x_0) = d, and ‖f‖ = 1, yielding the dual distance formula dist(x_0, M) = max{|f(x_0)| : f ∈ M^⊥, ‖f‖ ≤ 1}. Introduces annihilators S^⊥ ⊂ X* and pre-annihilators ^⊥F ⊂ X, proves cl(span S) = ^⊥(S^⊥), and extracts the fundamental density criterion (a subspace M is dense iff M^⊥ = {0}). Proves separability transfer—if X* is separable, then X is separable—by selecting unit vectors x_n with |f_n(x_n)| ≥ 1/2 for a dense sequence in S_{X*} and proving density of span{x_n} via annihilators, illustrating it by checking directly via {0, 1}^N that ℓ^∞ is non-separable and deducing that (ℓ^∞)* is non-separable. Enables the learner to prove density via annihilators, compute distances to subspaces dually, and separate points from closed subspaces. Leaves convex-set separation to an optional geometric Hahn-Banach lesson and bidual/adjoint theory to subsequent lessons.

nodes.label: Geometric Hahn-Banach and Hyperplane Separation
nodes.explanation: Optional enrichment building on the analytic Hahn-Banach extension theorem (and basic convexity in normed spaces) to establish hyperplane separation of convex sets. Introduces the Minkowski gauge p_C(x) = inf{t > 0 : x ∈ tC} of an absorbing convex set C, proving p_C is sublinear and that when C is open and contains 0, C = {x : p_C(x) < 1} with p_C(x) ≤ M‖x‖. Proves the first geometric Hahn-Banach theorem—two disjoint nonempty convex sets A and B with A open can be separated by a closed real hyperplane (Re f(a) < α ≤ Re f(b) for some nonzero f ∈ X*)—by translating A - B to contain 0 and applying analytic Hahn-Banach to its Minkowski gauge. Proves the second (strict) geometric Hahn-Banach theorem separating a closed convex set A from a disjoint compact convex set B by fattening B to an open convex set B + B(0, ε) disjoint from A. Deduces that every closed convex set is the intersection of all closed half-spaces containing it, and examines a counterexample in R^2 showing that two disjoint closed convex sets need not be strictly separable without compactness. Enables the learner to construct separating hyperplanes and verify separation hypotheses, without introducing weak topologies or Krein-Milman.

nodes.label: The Bidual, Canonical Embedding, and Reflexivity
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes norming functionals and closed-subspace separation from Hahn-Banach, classical sequence duals, and norm equivalence on finite-dimensional normed spaces (also using C([0, 1]) from earlier ancestors and norm-preserving extension from Hahn-Banach) to analyze the second dual X** = (X*)* and reflexivity. Defines the canonical evaluation map J : X → X** by (Jx)(f) = f(x) and uses norming functionals to prove J is a linear isometry (noting that cl(J(X)) ⊂ X** embeds any normed space isometrically as a dense subspace of a Banach space, and that J(X) is closed in X** whenever X is Banach). Defines reflexivity as surjectivity of the canonical map J—stressing that reflexivity requires J itself to be surjective, not merely an abstract isometric isomorphism X ≅ X**, and implies X is Banach. Proves that every finite-dimensional normed space is reflexive (using norm equivalence so X* coincides with the algebraic dual and dim X** = dim X) and that ℓ^p (1 < p < ∞) is reflexive (explicitly verifying that the classical dual identifications compose to J), whereas c_0 is non-reflexive since J identifies with the proper inclusion c_0 ↪ ℓ^∞. Proves two permanence theorems purely via Hahn-Banach without weak topologies: every closed subspace of a reflexive Banach space is reflexive, and a Banach space X is reflexive if and only if X* is reflexive. Deduces non-reflexivity of ℓ^1, ℓ^∞, and C([0, 1]) (by embedding c_0 isometrically into C([0, 1]) via disjoint tent functions). Enables the learner to test reflexivity of Banach spaces and apply hereditary duality properties, leaving weak compactness characterizations (Kakutani's theorem) to weak-topology modules.

nodes.label: Banach-Space Adjoint Operators and Annihilator Duality
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes Hahn-Banach norming functionals and annihilators with classical sequence duals (also using operator composition and invertibility from B(X, Y) and K^n norms from earlier ancestors) to develop the Banach-space adjoint T* : Y* → X* of T ∈ B(X, Y), defined by (T*g)(x) = g(Tx). Proves that T* ∈ B(Y*, X*), that T ↦ T* is linear (explicitly contrasting this with the conjugate-linear Hilbert-space adjoint), satisfies (ST)* = T*S*, I* = I, and (T^{-1})* = (T*)^{-1} when T is a bounded isomorphism, and is an isometry ‖T*‖ = ‖T‖ (using norming functionals for ‖T‖ ≤ ‖T*‖). Establishes the annihilator relations ker(T*) = (im T)^⊥ and cl(im T) = ^⊥(ker T*) (via Hahn-Banach), deducing that T has dense range if and only if T* is injective, and that dense range of T* implies injectivity of T while the converse can fail in non-reflexive spaces (verified concretely via T : ℓ^1 → ℓ^1, (Tx)_n = x_n/n, whose adjoint T* : ℓ^∞ → ℓ^∞ maps into c_0 ⊊ ℓ^∞). Computes explicit adjoints of matrices on K^n (transpose A^T under the bilinear pairing, not conjugate transpose), right and left shift operators, and diagonal operators on c_0 and ℓ^p (1 ≤ p < ∞). Enables the learner to compute concrete Banach-space adjoints and translate between injectivity and dense range via annihilators, leaving Hilbert-space adjoints and the Closed Range Theorem outside this lesson.

nodes.label: The Uniform Boundedness Principle (Banach-Steinhaus)
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes the Baire Category Theorem, Banach spaces, and bounded linear operators to prove the Uniform Boundedness Principle: if X is a Banach space, Y is a normed space, and F ⊂ B(X, Y) is pointwise bounded (sup_{T∈F} ‖Tx‖ < ∞ for every x ∈ X), then sup_{T∈F} ‖T‖ < ∞. Develops the proof by writing X = ⋃ F_n where F_n = {x : sup_{T∈F} ‖Tx‖ ≤ n} is closed, applying Baire Category to obtain a closed ball B[x_0, r] ⊂ F_{n_0}, and using linearity and translation (z = (x_0 + rz) - x_0 for ‖z‖ ≤ 1) to deduce ‖T‖ ≤ 2n_0/r uniformly. Derives the Banach-Steinhaus pointwise limit corollary: if T_n ∈ B(X, Y) converges pointwise on a Banach space X to T, then T ∈ B(X, Y) with ‖T‖ ≤ liminf ‖T_n‖ (contrasting pointwise convergence with operator-norm convergence). Demonstrates that completeness of X is indispensable via f_n(x) = n x_n on (c_00, ‖·‖_∞). Applies the theorem and its contrapositive to concrete problems: proving that a scalar sequence (y_n) satisfies ∑ |y_n| < ∞ whenever ∑ x_n y_n converges for all x ∈ c_0 (via partial-sum functionals), proving separate continuity implies joint continuity/boundedness for bilinear maps B : X × Y → Z when X is Banach, and deducing existence of divergence points from unbounded operator norms. Enables the learner to upgrade pointwise bounds to uniform operator-norm bounds and verify completeness hypotheses before applying Banach-Steinhaus.

nodes.label: The Open Mapping and Bounded Inverse Theorems
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes the Baire Category Theorem, Banach spaces (specifically the absolute convergence criterion), and bounded linear operators to prove the Open Mapping Theorem: every surjective T ∈ B(X, Y) between Banach spaces maps open sets to open sets. Explicitly separates the two roles of completeness in the proof: Stage 1 applies Baire Category to the Banach codomain Y = ⋃ cl(T(B_X(0, n))) together with linearity and scaling to obtain B_Y(0, δ) ⊂ cl(T(B_X(0, 1))); Stage 2 uses successive approximation and the absolute convergence criterion in the Banach domain X (building x = ∑ x_k with ‖x_k‖ < 2^{-(k-1)} and ‖y - T(∑_{j=1}^k x_j)‖ < δ 2^{-k}) to upgrade closure to the exact containment B_Y(0, δ) ⊂ T(B_X(0, 2)). Deduces the Bounded Inverse Theorem (a bijective bounded linear operator between Banach spaces is a bounded isomorphism) and the equivalence of comparable complete norms (if ‖·‖_1 and ‖·‖_2 are both Banach norms with ‖x‖_1 ≤ C‖x‖_2, they are equivalent). Contrasts with the incomplete-space counterexample id : (C([0, 1]), ‖·‖_∞) → (C([0, 1]), ‖·‖_1) to show completeness cannot be dropped. Enables the learner to prove bounded invertibility and norm equivalence between Banach spaces without estimating T^{-1} directly, leaving the Closed Graph Theorem to the next lesson.

nodes.label: The Closed Graph Theorem
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes product Banach spaces and the Bounded Inverse Theorem (and uses the established differentiation operator on (C^1([0, 1]), ‖·‖_∞) and concrete Banach spaces such as C([0, 1]) and c_0 from earlier ancestors) to prove and apply the Closed Graph Theorem. Defines the graph Γ(T) = {(x, Tx) : x ∈ X} ⊂ X × Y and its sequential closedness criterion (x_n → x and Tx_n → y imply y = Tx), carefully contrasting closedness of the graph with continuity (where x_n → x alone must force Tx_n to converge). Proves that a linear map T : X → Y between Banach spaces is bounded if and only if Γ(T) is closed in X × Y, using the completeness of the closed subspace Γ(T) under the graph norm ‖x‖_X + ‖Tx‖_Y and applying the Bounded Inverse Theorem to the bounded bijection π_X : Γ(T) → X so that T = π_Y ∘ π_X^{-1} is bounded. Diagnoses why completeness of the domain is essential via the differentiation operator D : (C^1([0, 1]), ‖·‖_∞) → (C([0, 1]), ‖·‖_∞), whose graph is closed by uniform convergence of derivatives yet which is unbounded because its domain is incomplete. Trains the Closed Graph Theorem as a practical tool for proving boundedness without directly estimating ‖Tx‖, through worked uses including showing a linear projection P^2 = P on a Banach space is bounded if and only if ker P and im P are both closed, and proving boundedness of linear maps into C([0, 1]) or c_0 with continuous point or coordinate evaluations. Enables the learner to verify boundedness via sequential graph closure and spot completeness failures.
